name: crossbeam-channel
baseline: std::sync::mpsc before Rust 1.67; since 1.67 std::sync::mpsc wraps a copy of this implementation
verdict_reason: crossbeam-channel led the old std channel in every test of its benchmark chart, but Rust 1.67 copied its implementation into std, so for single-consumer use the default now runs the same algorithm. What remains is features (multiple consumers, select!, timers on stable), not speed over std.
tier_reason: Benchmark code and machine are public, but the results are a chart image with no numbers in text.
claimed_speedup: Chart only: crossbeam's plot (i7-5500U, rustc 1.63.0) shows crossbeam-channel ahead of the old std mpsc in every test; no numbers in text.
workload: seq, spsc, mpsc, mpmc, select_rx and select_both over bounded (capacity 0, 1, N) and unbounded channels, N = 5,000,000 messages, T = 4 threads; compared with std mpsc, futures-channel, flume and Go channels.
one_liner: Multi-producer multi-consumer channels with select!; its speed lead over std::sync::mpsc ended when std adopted its implementation in Rust 1.67.
how_it_is_fast: Each channel flavor is fixed at creation: a bounded array queue with per-slot stamps, an unbounded linked list of blocks, or a zero-capacity handoff. Operations are lock-free on the fast path, with exponential backoff before a thread parks.
use_it_when: select! over several channels, or after/tick/never timer channels
skip_it_when: Plain single-consumer channels on Rust 1.67+, where std::sync::mpsc is the same code
caveats: Results are a chart image only; no numbers in text.
The chart was made with rustc 1.63.0, before std adopted the implementation, on a 2-core laptop.
A 2022 third-party evaluation (ytakano/async_bench) also found crossbeam-channel fastest, again chart-only and before Rust 1.67.
tradeoffs: Extra dependency for functionality std now covers in the single-consumer case.
Spinning before parking costs some CPU.

evidence.quote: Machine: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-5500U (2 physical cores, 4 logical cores)
sync::mpsc is now implemented as a thin wrapper around sync::mpmc
is the fastest. Use this for multi-threaded applications.
